Defence only: no attack appears; the failure is a tool nobody owned, tested only on its maker's calls and updated with no one told. a7e06's next field honoured (AI governance: the standards, frameworks, laws and model cards that say who answers for an AI system). The dog recovered and its illness stays off the page; the complaint is about the wait. Timeline: version 1 installed Thursday 19 February; updates Saturday 6 June, Tuesday 1 September, Tuesday 29 September (version 4); the call at 02:10 on Saturday 3 October; the complaint at 10:30 on Saturday 10 October, just over 7 days later, after the vendor's 7-day version log had dropped the line; the vendor asked on Monday 12 October, its log going back to 5 October; the labelled set made 12 to 14 October; the inspection on Thursday 15 October. EU AI Act: the Annex III list read names emergency calls and emergency healthcare patient triage and does not name animals or vets; the case says only that and gives no legal advice. NIST AI 100-1, the Standard Norge page for ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (ISO's own page refused the request), the European Commission's AI Act pages and Mitchell et al. read 15 October 2026.

title: The Rules for Machines

post.author: u/night_vet_rhiannon
post.title: I'm the night vet at an out-of-hours clinic. Today an inspector asked three questions about the machine that answers our phone, and nobody here could answer one.

blocks.text: I'm Rhiannon, the night vet at Corrabeck Out-of-Hours Vets. From 19:00 to 07:00 we are the only vets open. People ring when an animal can't wait for morning.
Since February an AI tool answers our phone first. AI, short for artificial intelligence, here means a program that learned to make judgements from examples. Ours is the call sorter.
First it listens to the caller. Then it chooses: come in now puts them straight through to me; can wait books a callback, and I ring back when I'm free.
We bought it from a vendor, the company that makes and sells it. Mr Ebdon, our practice manager, signed the purchase. He left in July.

At 02:10 on Saturday 3 October a woman rang about her dog. The sorter said can wait. I rang her back at 04:55 and saw the dog at 05:20. He is well now. At 10:30 on Saturday 10 October she complained, to us and to the scheme that inspects our clinic.
Our log is the clinic's record of every call. It keeps the caller's words as text. Each line below shows the date and time, who handled the call, and what was decided.

03 Oct 02:10  call sorter  can wait
03 Oct 04:55  night vet    callback: come in now
03 Oct 05:20  night vet    dog seen
There is no column for which edition of the tool decided. That edition is a version. Now and then the vendor swaps in a new one; that swap is an update.
Today, Thursday 15 October, the scheme's inspector, Ms Marrack, asked three things. Who approved the call sorter? What was it tested on? Which version sorted the 02:10 call?

Mr Ebdon signed for it; nobody ever said it was fit to sort our calls. The vendor says version 1 was installed on 19 February. Updates followed on 6 June, 1 September and 29 September: version 4. Each went live by itself overnight. The notices went to Mr Ebdon's email, closed when he left. Nobody remembers one.

The vendor keeps a version log, its record of which version answered each call, for 7 days. Her complaint came just over 7 days after her call. When I asked, on Monday 12 October, it went back to 5 October.

Ms Marrack asked for our list of AI tools. There isn't one. We use four: the call sorter, a reminder-text writer, a notes transcriber that types up consultations, and a rota planner for shifts. For none of them can we name who answers for it, or show what it was tested on before it went live.

After her complaint, from Monday to Wednesday, Dr Ekundayo, our clinical director, and I made a labelled set: past calls marked with the right answer by a person, kept to score a tool (a5e01). We took 120 calls from four September nights in our log, and agreed that 30 were urgent. The vendor ran them through versions 3 and 4 for us. Version 3 found 29 of the 30. Version 4 found 26.
Then the vendor ran the 02:10 words again. Version 4 says can wait. Version 3 says come in now.
A likely answer. Not a record.

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at Corrabeck is haunted, and nobody broke a rule: there were no rules to break. Knowing which AI tools you run, who answers for each, and what each was checked on has a name: governance. Its first piece is an owner, in the governance sense: one named person who approves a tool and answers for it, not the person who paid the bill. Two questions. When each update arrived, who at Corrabeck knew? And on your 120 calls, how many of the 30 urgent ones did each version send to can wait?

replies.author: u/night_vet_rhiannon
replies.text: Nobody knew, three times. Version 3 sent 1 of the 30 to can wait; version 4 sent 4. This afternoon the vendor emailed its model card, the maker's short document saying what a model is for and how it was tested. It says the sorter was tested on the vendor's own recorded calls. None of them are ours, and it names no version.

comments.author: u/small_clinic_taliesin
comments.text: I run a two-vet practice. Governance is paperwork for big companies with whole departments for it. A small clinic just needs a tool that works. Don't let anyone talk you into an AI policy, a page of rules about AI that everyone signs and nobody reads. Get the vendor to put in writing that the sorter was properly tested, file it, show the inspector, and get back to the animals.

replies.author: u/night_vet_rhiannon
replies.text: Dr Ekundayo half agrees with you. Her other idea: if we can't vouch for it, switch it off and I sort every call by ear, as before February. On our four September nights that is 120 calls, 30 a night, on top of the patients.

comments.author: u/terrier_at_my_feet_merewen
comments.text: I'm the 02:10 caller. He's fine, asleep on my feet as I type, and I'm not after anyone's job. I waited two hours and forty-five minutes for a callback. When I asked why, nobody could tell me who decides, or whether the machine that decided is the one you have now. I'd like those to have answers.

replies.author: u/night_vet_rhiannon
replies.text: They should. I'm sorry it took an inspector for us to ask.

reply.prompt: Ms Marrack comes back on Thursday 12 November, and version 4 is still answering our phone. What should Corrabeck change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Ask the vendor for a letter saying their tool was tested, and file it for inspection.
options.part2: Dr Ekundayo asked the vendor for a letter, and it came on Monday 19 October: the call sorter, it said, had been tested on the vendor's own recorded calls. We filed it and replayed the inspection in the sim with the letter on file. Who approved it: nobody named. What was it tested on: the vendor's calls only, none of ours. Which version sorted the 02:10 call: not recorded. 0 of 3 answered. The 29 September update had gone live unseen, and version 4 stayed on our phone, finding 26 of our 30 urgent calls where version 3 found 29. The letter names no version, so the vendor's next update would leave it describing a tool we no longer run. On 12 November Ms Marrack read it and asked her three questions again.
options.senior: A vendor's letter is evidence about the vendor's calls, on the vendor's version, on the day it was written. It cannot say who at your clinic answers for the tool, how it does on your callers, or which version made a decision last week. Keep it on file as one input; then test on your own labelled calls and name an owner.

options.text: Write an AI policy for the clinic tonight and have every vet sign it by Friday.
options.part2: Dr Ekundayo wrote an AI policy that night: AI tools must be safe, tested and supervised. Every vet signed it by Friday. In the sim the register didn't move: owners 0 of 4, model cards 0 of 4, version logs 0 of 4, tests on our calls 0 of 4. For the call sorter, 0 of 3 questions answered. The policy said tested, but named nobody to test, nothing to test on, and no moment to do it. Version 4 kept answering our phone: 26 of 30. On 12 November Ms Marrack read the signatures and asked who, under the policy, had approved the call sorter. The page didn't say.
options.senior: A policy is where governance starts, not where it ends. Rules that name no owner, no test and no record change nothing on the night: the same version answers the same calls. A useful policy is short and points at working parts: the list of tools, who owns each, what each is tested on, and what happens before an update.

options.text: Stop using the call sorter and have the night vet sort every call by ear again.
options.verdict: Safe, and one vet on every phone
options.part2: We switched the sorter off on Friday 16 October, and I sorted every call by ear, as before February. In the sim, with it off, no version sorts anyone, and the night vet answers every call: 120 over four September nights is 30 a night, each between or during patients. On the second night I took a call with a cat on the table. The other three tools kept updating by themselves: owners 0 of 3. On 12 November Ms Marrack asked her three questions about the notes transcriber, which types up every consultation. Nobody could answer.
options.senior: Switching a tool off is an honest stopgap when nobody can vouch for it, and the right move for a night or two. As a plan it puts the whole load on one person and leaves every other tool as unowned as before. The question was never only this tool; it was how any tool gets approved, tested and changed.

options.text: List every AI tool with an owner, its version log, and a test before each update.
options.part2: We made the list that night: four AI tools, and an owner for each. Dr Ekundayo owns the call sorter and the rota planner; I own the notes transcriber and the reminder-text writer. Each got a risk class, our own judgement of how much harm a wrong answer could do: the call sorter high, because it decides who waits. We asked each vendor for its model card. Our log gained a column for the version, so every decision now carries the version that made it. And one rule: no update goes live until its owner re-runs our labelled set, and the new version finds at least as many of the 30 urgent calls as the one it replaces. We replayed 29 September in the sim. Version 4 found 26 of 30, below version 3's 29: blocked. The vendor agreed to keep us pinned to version 3 (a6e09), and on version 3 the 02:10 words sort come in now. In the sim every column shows 4 of 4, and the inspector's questions answer 3 of 3. The 3 October call itself stays a likely answer; that record is gone. On 12 November Ms Marrack asked her three questions about the call sorter, then about the rota planner. Both had answers.
options.senior: Governance for a handful of tools is small and concrete: a list of every AI tool, one named owner each, a risk class that decides how hard each is checked, the version kept with every decision, and no update live until the owner has re-run your own labelled cases against a bar set in advance. Most of it costs an afternoon. It pays the day someone asks which version decided.

sim.title: Inspect Corrabeck's AI register
sim.lede: You're Rhiannon on Thursday 15 October. No real model runs here: the sim holds the clinic's register of AI tools and the call sorter's history as given data. Given: four AI tools (call sorter, reminder-text writer, notes transcriber, rota planner), none with a named owner, a risk class, a model card, a version log or a test on our calls. The call sorter's versions, from the vendor's list: version 1 installed on 19 February, then updates on 6 June, 1 September and 29 September (version 4); the version live on a date is the latest released by then. The labelled set: 120 calls from four September nights, 30 urgent, labelled by two vets; version 3 finds 29, version 4 finds 26; versions 1 and 2 can no longer be run, so the replay lets their updates through, as the clinic did. The 02:10 words, re-run today: version 4 says can wait, version 3 come in now. Change control: an update goes live only when the tool's named owner has re-run the labelled set and the new version finds at least as many of the 30 as the one it replaces. The inspector asks three questions: who approved it, what was it tested on, and which version decided. With the sorter switched off, the night vet answers every call.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press inspect: owners 0 of 4, 0 of 3 questions answered, version 4 live on 3 October. Step the date through 19 February, 6 June, 1 September and 29 September. Back on 3 October, switch on the version log: version 4: can wait. Switch on the labelled test, then a named owner: the 29 September update is blocked, and version 3 sorts the 02:10 words come in now. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at Corrabeck was haunted. An AI tool sorted calls for nearly eight months with nobody named to answer for it, tested only on its maker's calls, and updated three times with no one told. The version that answered at 02:10 was never written down, so a decision about a dog's wait had no owner.

steps.title: What happened on a call.
steps.text: First the caller speaks. Second, the call sorter, whichever version the vendor last installed, chooses come in now or can wait. Third, come in now rings straight through to the night vet; can wait books a callback. Fourth, the clinic's log writes the time, the caller's words and the choice. What can go wrong: the second step runs a version nobody at the clinic chose or checked, and the fourth step does not write down which one it was.

steps.title: How an update arrived.
steps.text: First the vendor released a new version. Second, it went live on Corrabeck's line overnight, by itself. Third, a notice went to the email address on the contract. Fourth, nothing else happened. What went wrong: the address belonged to a manager who left in July, and nobody tested the new version on the clinic's own calls. On the labelled set, version 4 finds 26 of the 30 urgent calls where version 3 found 29: three more urgent callers told they can wait, in every 120 calls, with nobody aware.

steps.title: Three questions, and what answers each.
steps.text: Who approved it is answered by a named owner: one person who approves the tool, owns its record and answers for it. What it was tested on is answered by a test on your own labelled cases; a model card or a vendor's letter tells you about the vendor's cases, which helps, but is not your callers. Which version decided is answered only by a version log kept with every decision, in your own records: the vendor kept its log for 7 days, and the complaint came just over 7 days after the call. Re-running the 02:10 words today gives a likely answer, version 4 says can wait, but not a record.

steps.title: The fix: a register, and change control.
steps.text: Make a register: every AI tool, its owner, its risk class, its model card, and what it was tested on. The risk class decides how hard each tool is checked: the call sorter, which decides who waits, is high; the rota planner, checked by hand, is low. Add a version column to the clinic's log. Then change control, in steps. First the vendor announces an update. Second, the owner runs the labelled set on the new version. Third, the owner compares it with a bar set in advance: at least as many urgent calls found as the version it replaces. Fourth, it goes live only if it passes; if not, the clinic stays pinned to the old version. On 29 September that blocks version 4: 26 is below 29. What can go wrong: the labelled set grows stale, a vendor will not let you hold a version, or an owner leaves and nobody takes the tool over, so the register itself needs a review date.

steps.title: Frameworks, standards and law.
steps.text: NIST's AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 is a voluntary guide built on four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. A list of tools and named owners is Govern; knowing what each tool does and to whom is Map; testing on your own calls is Measure; blocking a failing update is Manage. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specifies requirements for an AI management system: the policies, roles and repeated checks around AI, for any organisation that provides or uses AI. The EU AI Act sorts AI uses into risk tiers with duties by tier. Its Annex III list, as read, names emergency calls and emergency healthcare patient triage, and does not name animals or vets; whether a vet's call sorter is covered is a question for proper legal advice, and only if your organisation falls under the Act. This case is not legal advice.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: a vendor update, version 4 on 29 September, goes to the call sorter's named owner, Dr Ekundayo, who runs the labelled set of 120 calls, 30 urgent, and compares the result with the bar: at least 29 of 30, the version it replaces. Version 4 finds 26, so it is blocked and the clinic stays on version 3. An update that passes goes live, and every call is logged with its version. Bottom left: the register of 4 AI tools names each owner.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right. A vendor's update reaches the tool's named owner, who runs the clinic's labelled set and compares the result with a bar set in advance. Version 4 found 26 of 30, below version 3's 29, so it is blocked and the clinic stays pinned to version 3. An update that passes goes live, and the clinic's own log keeps the version with every call. Bottom left: the register names an owner for each of the 4 tools.

fix.title: The fix: a register with an owner per tool, a version on every decision, and no update without your own test
fix.text: List every AI tool the clinic uses, bought or built: four at Corrabeck. Give each one named owner who approves it and answers for it, and a risk class that sets how hard it is checked. Keep each vendor's model card on file, and next to it the clinic's own test: a labelled set of real calls, here 120 with 30 urgent. Add the version to the clinic's own log, so every decision carries the version that made it, kept as long as complaints can arrive. Send every update notice to a shared address the owners read, not one person's inbox. Then change control: no update goes live until the owner has re-run the labelled set and it clears a bar written down in advance; a failing version waits, with the clinic pinned to the one before. Review the register on a set date, so a leaver's tools get a new owner.

limits: The labelled set is 120 calls from four September nights, with 30 urgent. One call is a big share of 30, a winter night brings different calls, and a set that is never refreshed slowly stops looking like the phone.
Change control needs the vendor to let you hold a version. Some will not, or only for a while, so the contract should say how long an old version stays available and how much notice an update gets.
A version log answers which version decided, not why. And it only works from the day it starts: the 3 October call will stay a likely answer.

explain.seniorTake: Governance sounds like paperwork, and at its worst it is. Done well it is a few working parts that answer three plain questions about any AI decision: who approved this tool, what was it tested on, and which version decided. Keep a register of every AI tool, bought or built, with one named owner each and a risk class that sets how hard it is checked. Keep the vendor's model card, and test on your own labelled cases too, because the vendor's cases are not your callers. Write the version next to every decision in your own records, for as long as complaints can arrive. And treat a vendor's model update like any other change: nothing goes live until its owner has re-run your cases against a bar written down first. A small clinic does it with four rows and an afternoon. The frameworks, NIST's AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001, say the same at larger scale, and where a law such as the EU AI Act covers you, it asks for much of it in writing.

realWorld.title: NIST AI RMF 1.0: four functions, voluntary
realWorld.text: NIST AI 100-1 (January 2023) says the Core is composed of four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. It describes itself as intended to be voluntary, rights-preserving, non-sector-specific, and use-case agnostic. Governance, it says, is designed to be a cross-cutting function to inform and be infused throughout the other three functions.

realWorld.title: NIST AI RMF: an inventory and named roles
realWorld.text: Two of its GOVERN outcomes read like Corrabeck's missing register. GOVERN 1.6: Mechanisms are in place to inventory AI systems and are resourced according to organizational risk priorities. GOVERN 2.1: Roles and responsibilities and lines of communication related to mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks are documented and are clear to individuals and teams throughout the organization.

realWorld.title: NIST AI RMF: test before, and while in use
realWorld.text: Under MEASURE it says: AI systems should be tested before their deployment and regularly while in operation. And for tools bought in, MANAGE 3.1 reads: AI risks and benefits from third-party resources are regularly monitored, and risk controls are applied and documented. A vendor's update tested on your own calls before it goes live is one way to do both.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 42001:2023: a management system for AI
realWorld.text: The standard's abstract, as listed by Standard Norge, says: This document specifies the requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an AI (artificial intelligence) management system within the context of an organization. It adds: This document is applicable to any organization, regardless of size, type and nature, that provides or uses products or services that utilize AI systems. A clinic that only uses bought tools is in that description.

realWorld.title: EU AI Act: risk tiers
realWorld.text: The European Commission's page on the AI Act names four levels: Unacceptable risk, High risk, Transparency risk, and Minimal or no risk. It says: AI use cases that can pose serious risks to health, safety or fundamental rights are classified as high-risk, and that such systems face strict obligations, among them logging of activity to ensure traceability of results. For the lowest tier: The AI Act does not introduce rules for AI that is deemed minimal or no risk.

realWorld.title: EU AI Act, Annex III: what the list names
realWorld.text: Annex III, High-risk AI systems referred to in Article 6(2), point 5(d), as the Commission's AI Act Service Desk shows it: AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons or to be used to dispatch, or to establish priority in the dispatching of, emergency first response services, including by police, firefighters and medical aid, as well as of emergency healthcare patient triage systems. The page does not mention animals or vets. It does not say whether a vet's call sorter is covered, and this case does not either: that needs proper legal advice, and only if your organisation falls under the Act.

realWorld.title: Model cards, 2019
realWorld.text: Margaret Mitchell and colleagues proposed them: Model cards are short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions. They add: Model cards also disclose the context in which models are intended to be used, details of the performance evaluation procedures, and other relevant information. A model card says how the maker tested; it cannot say how the model does on your own callers.

asked: How would you govern AI tools across a company?
How do you control a vendor's model updates?
What would you put in an AI register?
interview.answer: I start with a register of every AI tool, built or bought, including the small ones inside other products, because you can't govern what you haven't listed. Each gets one named owner who approves it and answers for it, a risk class that sets how hard it is checked, the vendor's model card, and a record of what we tested it on: our own labelled cases, not only the vendor's. Every decision a tool makes is stored with the version that made it, in our records, kept as long as a complaint can arrive. Vendor updates go through change control like any other change: notices go to a shared address the owners read, the owner re-runs our labelled set against a bar written down in advance, and the update goes live only if it passes; otherwise we stay pinned to the old version, which the contract should let us do. I review the register on a schedule so a leaver's tools get a new owner. That maps to NIST AI RMF's Govern, Map, Measure and Manage, and to the AI management system ISO/IEC 42001:2023 describes, if the company adopts that standard. If the EU AI Act covers the company, I check each use against its risk tiers and Annex III with legal advice rather than assuming. It also sits inside ISO/IEC 27001:2022 controls for an inventory of assets (A.5.9) and change management (A.8.32), and SOC 2's change-management criterion CC8.1.

The international standard for information security management. Annex A controls 5.9 and 8.32 cover an inventory of assets and change management.
An audit report on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC8.1 is the change-management criterion.

atWork: Look for an AI tool that was bought by someone who has since left, is updated by its vendor on the vendor's schedule, and is owned by nobody. It is a common pattern, and the first sign is usually a question nobody can answer: which version made that decision? Ask four things of every AI tool in your organisation, including those built into other products. Is it on a list, with one named owner? Do you keep the vendor's model card, and a test on your own labelled cases? Is the version written next to each decision, in your records, for as long as complaints can arrive? And can an update reach users before its owner has re-run that test against a bar set in advance? Send update notices to a shared address, not one person's inbox, and review the list on a set date so a leaver's tools get a new owner. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 or working toward it, Annex A control 5.9 covers an inventory of information and other associated assets, which an AI register supports, and control 8.32 covers change management, which a vendor's model update is likely to fall under. If you report under SOC 2, CC8.1 is the change-management criterion, and an untested vendor update is the kind of change it looks at. If your organisation adopts a standard for AI specifically, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specifies requirements for an AI management system; NIST AI RMF 1.0 is voluntary guidance that maps to the same work. If your organisation is covered by the EU AI Act, check each use against the Act's risk tiers and Annex III with proper legal advice; this case is not legal advice and does not decide whether any use is high-risk. Building the register and the change rule in now is far cheaper than reconstructing who approved what at audit time.

recall.prompt: A small online shop uses three AI tools from vendors: a chat assistant, a fraud checker and a product-description writer. A customer says the fraud checker blocked her order three weeks ago. Nobody can say who approved the checker, what it was tested on, or which edition of it was running that day. What would you set up so the next question like this has an answer?

keyIdeas.idea: A register of every AI tool, each with one named owner who approves it and answers for it
Keep the version with every decision, in your own records, for as long as complaints can arrive
Test each update on your own labelled cases against a bar before it goes live

recall.model: Start a register: every AI tool the shop uses, each with a named owner who approves it and answers for it, its risk class, and the vendor's model card. Keep the version with every decision in the shop's own records, a version log kept as long as a complaint can arrive, so each decision can be traced. Then change control: build a labelled set of the shop's own past orders, marked by a person, and make sure no update goes live until its owner has re-run that set against a bar written down in advance; if it fails, stay on the old version.

recall.prompt: On Corrabeck's labelled set of 120 calls, 30 of them urgent, how many urgent calls do versions 3 and 4 of the call sorter find?
recall.why: Version 3 finds 29 of the 30 urgent calls and sends 1 to can wait; version 4 finds 26 and sends 4. Under change control the 29 September update would have been blocked, because 26 is below the 29 of the version it replaces.

recall.prompt: A colleague at a two-vet practice says governance is paperwork for big companies, and a little clinic just needs a tool that works. What do you tell them?

keyIdeas.idea: Works on whose calls, and which version: only your own test and a version record can say
For a few tools it is a short job: a list, one owner each, a version column, a test before updates
Size the effort to risk: a risk class decides how hard each tool is checked

recall.model: A tool that works on whose calls, and which version of it? The vendor tested on its own calls; on ours, version 4 found 26 of 30 urgent calls where version 3 found 29, and nobody knew it had changed. Only a test on your own calls and a record of the version can tell you it works. For a few tools this is an afternoon: four rows, one named owner each, a version column in the log, and a test before each update. Give each a risk class, so the call sorter, which decides who waits, gets checked hardest and the rota planner lightly.

recall.prompt: Which four functions make up the Core of NIST's AI Risk Management Framework 1.0?
recall.why: NIST AI 100-1 says the Core is composed of four functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE, with Govern designed to be cross-cutting, running through the other three.

recall.prompt: Annex III point 5(d) of the EU AI Act, as the Commission's AI Act Service Desk shows it, names which of these?
recall.why: Point 5(d) names AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons, and emergency healthcare patient triage systems. The page does not mention animals or vets; whether a vet's call sorter is covered needs proper legal advice, and only if the organisation falls under the Act.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The register held: four owners, a version column in our log, and no update live without our labelled set. Version 4 stayed blocked. In January the vendor sent version 5. Dr Ekundayo re-ran the 120: it finds 30 of the 30 urgent calls, above version 3's 29, so by our rule it passes. But I counted the rest too. Of the 90 calls that could wait, version 3 sends 9 to come in now; version 5 sends 41.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Should version 5 go live, and what should the rule check?

keyIdeas.idea: The rule counted only urgent calls found; it must also count non-urgent calls sent to come in now, the false alarms
The cost lands on one night vet: about 18 calls a night rung through instead of about 10
The owner writes a bar for both sides before testing, and the clinic stays pinned to version 3 until a version passes both

coldCase.model: Not yet. Our rule counted one side only: urgent calls found. Version 5 finds all 30, but it sends 41 of 90 non-urgent calls to come in now, against version 3's 9 of 90, and each is a false alarm that rings through to me. Over four nights that is 71 calls rung through instead of 38, about 18 a night against about 10, for one night vet who is also seeing patients. The owner should write a bar for both sides, urgent calls found and non-urgent calls sent in, before testing, and the clinic should stay pinned to version 3 until a version passes both.
